defect.evidence_quote: the Police Department’s procedures mandated the opening of closed containers and the listing of their contents.
defect.problem: The holding field is truncated with an ellipsis and omits necessary limitations: standardized container-opening procedures, good faith administration, and no investigatory pretext/sole-purpose investigation.
defect.proposed_fix: Replace the holding with: Inventory searches of impounded vehicles, including opening closed containers, are reasonable when conducted under standardized procedures that govern container-opening, are administered in good faith, and are not a pretext or sole-purpose criminal investigation.

reasons: The opinion supports container-opening only in the context of standardized procedures: “procedures mandated the opening of closed containers and the listing of their contents.”

The opinion also requires good faith/noninvestigatory administration: “there was no showing that the police, who were following standardized procedures, acted in bad faith or for the sole purpose of investigation.”
residual_risks: As written, the ellipsis makes the holding too incomplete to stand without repair.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: State the full rule instead of using an ellipsis, and include good faith plus non-pretext limitations.

reasons: The opinion states that “inventory searches are now a well-defined exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment.”
The case specifically refines inventory-search doctrine for closed containers and standardized police discretion after Opperman and Lafayette.

reviewed.suggested_tightening: Could specify the role as Key — closed-container and standardized-discretion refinement.
